[This is a guest post by the MathHelm scientific committee, whose membership is listed at the bottom of this post. -T.]

Mathematics depends on our regular conversations with colleagues and with the wider public. They help us share ideas, deepen our collective understanding, see where the field stands, and decide what to explore next. They also keep us connected. As technology changes rapidly, talking through uncertainty and supporting one another matter for our well-being and our shared effort to understand the universe.

On October 6, 2026, OpenAI released 722 mathematical manuscripts generated by an internal AI model, claiming significant results across many research areas. This release will undoubtedly bring significant changes to the mathematical community, even though most of these papers were not verified by us humans and among them, many results did not have a companion lean-verification.

Like many others, I was interested in several of these papers. I also found the whole collection intimidating. Their presentations often differ from the scholarly conventions I knew, and I could not quickly assess most of the arguments on my own. It was natural that I wanted to discuss with colleagues, but often felt hesitant to speak before I felt confident in my judgment. Sometimes I wasn’t even sure whom to discuss with. A few colleagues felt the same way. Together, we created MathHelm: a place for everyone to share comments, ask questions, and think together on massive AI-generated papers, including these 722 papers and any other similar paper.

Each of us only has the expertise to assess a small part of such a broad collection. Useful discussions were already appearing online: explanations of an idea, questions about a proof, or missed connections to earlier or ongoing work and related concerns. People’s comments are scattered and easy to miss. Bringing them together saves time for everyone and gives the community a clearer picture.

MathHelm is open to researchers worldwide, with discussions primarily in English. We invite mathematical researchers to register under their real names and discuss AI-generated papers and related mathematical questions. Comments can address correctness, readability, originality, main results, or key ideas. We hope everyone could be as objective and specific as possible, and include references where appropriate. You can also upload your own PDF notes.

The forum was founded by the scientific committee listed below and operates on a nonprofit basis to serve the mathematical community. It focuses on mathematical content and takes no predetermined position for or against AI. Our policy prohibits any organization from using forum content to train AI models.

Our guiding principle is simple:

Mathematicians have no obligation to check AI-generated papers. But if you happen to read part of one, your observations may be valuable to the whole community.

Even small comments such as a question about the proof method, an explanation of a single step, or a useful reference can help. You do not need a verdict on an entire paper to join the conversation.

Whatever tools we use, mathematics should remain a shared human pursuit: people should be able to understand its ideas, question its claims, and help shape its future. We hope MathHelm can offer a little steadiness in this age of rapid change, and a place to keep learning from one another.

Liang Xiao (Peking University)

— 2. Pseudodifferential operators —

In the previous set of notes we established constructed a reasonably large class of CZOs, namely the Hörmander-Mikhlin multipliers. These multipliers suffice for the analysis of translation-invariant settings, such as studying operators arising from constant-coefficient differential operators such as the Laplacian. However they are not general enough to handle non-translation-invariant situations. For this, we must turn to the pseudodifferential operators, which generalise the variable-coefficient differential operators when the coefficients are smooth.

To motivate these operators, we begin with the Fourier inversion formula

(In the theory of semiclassical analysis, it is often customary to introduce a small parameter , called Planck’s constant, and replace in the above equation by , but we will not do so here.) By expanding out the Fourier transform and interchanging integrals, we (formally) have

The operators generalise both spatial multipliers and Fourier multipliers , at least when the symbol is smooth. The map from symbol to operator is linear. However, in contrast to the homomorphism laws

for smooth multipliers of space or frequency only, it is not quite true that the quantization operation preserves products:

Indeed, this would imply in particular that any two operators and commute, which is untrue (indeed, and themselves do not commute with each other). Roughly speaking, the Kohn-Nirenberg quantization always arranges the factors to the “left” of the factors, whereas the Weyl quantization spreads them around evenly. One can obtain partial substitutes of the homomorphism law; for instance, it is still true that if does not depend on , or does not depend on . These types of observations form the foundation for the pseudodifferential symbol calculus, which is a very useful tool for analysing variable-coefficient linear differential operators (especially those with smooth elliptic symbols), although we will only touch on the foundations of that vast subject here.

There are two main aspects to the theory of pseudodifferential operators: the analytic aspects, in which the boundedness properties of operators are analysed, and the (mainly) algebraic aspects, in which one learns how to compose, commute, or invert operators (usually modulo lower order terms). We shall begin with the analytic aspects.

— 2.1. Symbol classes —

Of course, to get any sort of usable bound on the operators , we shall need some quantitative control on the symbol . This requires placing in one of the symbol classes. There are quite a variety of symbol classes to use, which determine the growth and regularity of the symbol in both the spatial variable and the frequency variable . For simplicitly, we shall stick here with the standard symbol class , which suffices for the local theory of elliptic variable coefficient operators with smooth coefficients. (These are also called the classical symbol classes, but this is confusing, given that the distinction between classical and quantum mechanics in this subject.) Each symbol class represents a decomposition of phase space into regions respecting the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, with the symbol required to be smoothly adapted to each such region and have a certain upper bound on amplitude. In this case, the relevant regions of phase space are the regions where the spatial variable is localised to a ball of radius , and the frequency variable is localised to a dyadic annulus .

— 3. Sobolev spaces —

With all the various inequalities at our disposal (the Hörmander-Mikhlin multiplier theorem, the Calderón-Vaillancourt theorem, and the Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality) we can now quickly develop some of the classical theory of homogeneous and inhomogeneous Sobolev spaces on Euclidean spaces ; of course we will not attempt an exhaustive survey of this vast subject here. In particular, we omit one important analytical aspect of these spaces, namely their local stability under smooth diffeomorphisms, which allows one to transplant these spaces onto manifolds and thus have application to various problems in differential geometry. item.title: Lean Grimoire
item.dc:creator: Terence Tao
item.description: Back in July, I started experimenting with using modern coding agents to build a number of mathematical visualization applets. With the extremely hectic events of the last few months, I had to set those projects aside; but I recently found a bit of time to work on one such project that I had started back […]
item.content:encoded:
Back in July, I started experimenting with using modern coding agents to build a number of mathematical visualization applets. With the extremely hectic events of the last few months, I had to set those projects aside; but I recently found a bit of time to work on one such project that I had started back then, which was to modernize a Javascript interactive textbook I had made back in 2018, entitled “QED”, and announced previously on this blog. The purpose of that textbook was to teach propositional and first-order logic in the form of a “crafting game”, where one applied various rules of logic to reach a desired conclusion from a given set of hypotheses.

With a coding agent, I rebuilt the game (which I have given the working title of “Lean Grimoire”) with a number of new features, for instance giving the option to show an in-progress Lean proof of one’s game state. Just for fun, I also added an option to play in a “fantasy mode” in which various game elements are depicted using fantasy-themed flavor text (for instance, mathematical statements become “potions”, mathematical expressions become “scrolls”, and so forth). Here is a typical screenshot, in which one has nearly completed the proof of the assertion given :

I would be interested in having some playtesting of this app to make it more useful as a means to teach logical proofs and/or Lean.

This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] In late September and early October, we distributed a survey of early career mathematicians. Our goals were to take a “temperature check” of the […]
item.content:encoded:
[This is a guest post by Anna Brandenberger, Hanna Mularczyk, and Dora Woodruff (MIT). This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

In late September and early October, we distributed a survey of early career mathematicians. Our goals were to take a “temperature check” of the community, and to give early career mathematicians a centralized, targeted platform to share their views on AI (the survey was not a rigorous data analysis effort). The personal stakes are highest for grad students and postdocs, who face job insecurity and funding instability, so it’s important that our voices are taken into account. We worry that our concerns will be deprioritized, or even misrepresented, without collective resources like this survey.

On October 29th, we posted the results of this survey to the arXiv (history and overview). In the end, over 260 mathematicians filled out the survey, representing around 60 institutions and at least 5 countries. Many of them left free responses in addition to answering the multiple choice questions.

This blog post is an invitation to take a look at the survey results. Some of the results surprised and/or dismayed us: in particular, Question 3.2, Question 3.3, Question 5.2, and Question 6.1, which concern career outlook and research motivation. It’s also important to point out that nearly all of the responses were collected before October 6th, capturing a sample of thoughts from a specific context: we nervously wonder how different this data would look today. As journals, hiring committees, and faculty members make decisions about the future, we urge them to take these survey results into account — and to continue fostering discussions between senior and junior mathematicians.

item.title: What should we teach our (undergraduate) students?
item.dc:creator: Terence Tao
item.description: [This is a guest post by Jana Gevertz and Steffen Marcus. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] In the last few months AI has hit our discipline with a frightening force. Many of us, understandably, have turned our attention to our students. They are […]
item.content:encoded:
[This is a guest post by Jana Gevertz and Steffen Marcus. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

In the last few months AI has hit our discipline with a frightening force. Many of us, understandably, have turned our attention to our students. They are absorbing this change while still working out what kind of mathematicians, and what kind of professionals, they hope to become. On this blog, Álvaro Lozano-Robledo recently asked “what should we tell our students?” (What should we tell our students? | What’s new). In this post, we will focus on the natural follow-up question: “what should we teach them?”

Whatever our students choose for their future careers, be it academia or industry, their work will continue to depend on the depth of their mathematical understanding. However, more and more of that work will likely involve prompting, interpreting, checking, and communicating mathematical ideas that an AI model helped generate. Mathematical understanding as we have come to teach it is built on a time-honored tradition of exercise, proof, and computation: struggle with hard problems until a discovery is made, develop a conjecture and make an effort to prove it, compute by hand to uncover a desired result or a pattern that reveals itself. How will our students build mathematical understanding when AI tools can automate the very processes needed to develop it? What does it mean to train new mathematicians?

Presuming society continues to cede more decisions and reasoning to AI, it has been rightly argued that it would be dangerous for these decisions to “rest on reasons that no human community understands” (We’re gonna need a lot more mathematicians | What’s new). In mathematics, as in many other academic communities, understanding begins with undergraduate training that builds off years of education at the primary and secondary level. Without thriving undergraduate mathematics programs, the mathematics community is at risk of depleting the pool of individuals with the capacity to assess work done with (or by) AI and to set the directions of the field.

However, undergraduate education is at an impasse. In our liberal arts style college here in New Jersey, we have struggled with the practical implications of AI on our classrooms while circling more broadly around the question of how our curriculum must change for the future. There is a visceral feeling that our courses need to change, but it’s not clear what that change should look like. The discipline’s conversations so far have centered on our research and publications, our early career colleagues, and our graduate students. The 2026 AMS Committee on Education Workshop Report (2026 AMS Committee on Education Workshop Report | What’s new) highlights the beginning of our efforts to reorganize graduate level curricula with AI in mind. We believe a parallel and continuous effort focused on our undergraduate programs is needed.

This is especially important for our students entering graduate school, as they will be interfacing with mathematics differently than we have in the past. If it is true that “we won’t get to be heroes anymore” (When AI comes for Your Purpose in Life – The New York Times) and we will begin working in larger teams along with AI systems to develop new ideas and proofs, then our training needs to be focused on understanding and robustly checking results presented to us in slightly “alien” forms.

The central problem: teaching understanding

Luckily, this is not really a completely new way of thinking and teaching. After all, undergraduate training has always been about teaching students to check, interpret, and explain results already known to other mathematicians. Whether it be calculations that have been executed time and time again, or proofs of important theorems that are well-established, undergraduate students learn mathematics and shape their understanding using pre-existing knowledge. From that perspective, the basic skills used to interpret, understand, and communicate mathematics learned through an AI system are already a central piece of undergraduate curricula.

However, we cannot simply continue to ignore this technology as a nuisance to our ability to assign homework exercises and hope for the best. We must teach students to work with these systems. And we must find the right way to do so without offloading their ability to think through problems on their own. Our students need both the skillset and the experience necessary to critically validate AI outputs. Whether we like it or not, they will be expected to work in this way with AI systems in their careers. Our coursework needs to carefully train them to develop mathematical intuition, reasoning, and computational skills in concert with this new technology, rather than apart from it, as is our current instinct.

Our pre-AI experience shows that there are distinct differences between productively struggling to re-create existing knowledge and using technology to do this work. Consider an undergraduate student learning strategies of integration in a calculus class. From the student’s perspective, there is something distinctly different about identifying the substitution that transforms a seemingly “impossible” integral into an easily solvable one versus reading through a solution where the substitution has been selected. A student who considered the structure of the integrand to identify an appropriate substitution would indeed have created the result for themselves, despite the expected substitution being well known. A student who instead blindly followed a computer’s (or even their instructor’s) approach without investigating will likely not internalize that changing variables is a foundational mathematical technique that maps difficult problems onto solvable problems.

This is a small example of the difference between teaching the concept versus teaching the computation. This battle has been playing out in our discussions of pedagogy and content since symbolic computation software have become widespread. What has changed is that this conflict has now expanded to the advanced levels of our undergraduate curricula — the newest AI models have come to make our courses a push-button exercise. If our students rely on reading out computer generated proofs and computations exercise by exercise, they immediately lose the critical moments of productive struggle necessary to build mathematical understanding.

Where do we go from here?

As with any debate, there are those who will passionately argue both extremes. Some will say we simply must eschew AI technology by continuing to teach as we always have, relying on in-class pen and paper assessments. This approach fails to prepare our students for a future in which they will need to work efficiently with AI models and manage their output. Others will argue we should throw away our outdated curricula and embrace the transformative power of AI. The risk in this approach is the outsourcing of student learning and understanding, a risk that is simply too high. The answer must lie somewhere subtly in the middle of these two extremes.

In her recent post on this blog (AI, Mathematics, Education, and a public goods problem | What’s New), Gireeja Ranade argues that “we must teach harder, better, and stronger”. Ranade identifies the central issue facing our community as we learn how to teach our students to work with AI models: “we need to train students so that they know what they know and don’t know — students who can identify proof by intimidation and by authority, and have the confidence to push back.” Looking around, it seems the natural inclination for many of us is to revert to how we have taught in the past (perhaps “harder, better, and stronger”) and to ignore the power of AI within the confines of the classroom. Most of us are quietly choosing one of the two extremes.

Indeed, as authors of this post ourselves, we have yet to find the right way to incorporate AI in our mathematical biology or geometry classes this semester, though we have been thinking about it for a while. Adjusting an undergraduate curriculum is difficult and time-consuming work that cannot simply be done on top of the full-time job faculty already do. Reaching a consensus is also going to be very challenging, and even once a curriculum is agreed upon, the work that must follow to redesign course materials is substantial. For these reasons, it is easy to let our undergraduate courses wait three, four, or five more years until we see how everything shakes out. However, our students desperately need us to find this delicate balance more quickly. They need to acquire a breadth of experience interfacing with these systems in their mathematical work now, or they risk getting left behind.

And therein lies the challenge: how do we design undergraduate mathematics curricula that takes such a balanced approach? There have been a number of recent summits, reports, and statements regarding how AI is changing the mathematical landscape and how we should respond. Similar concerted efforts with a focus on undergraduate education are necessary. The MAA Statement on AI in Higher Education outlines some top-down beliefs on how the undergraduate curriculum may have to change. However, much more activity is needed to help guide department leaders and educators on how to make these suggestions concrete. Together we need to work towards a modernized curriculum that considers the following questions.

  • How do we design and implement a curriculum that places a greater emphasis on higher-order competencies, including conceptual and computational reasoning as well as problem solving and modeling (per: MAA Statement on AI)? Efforts to change curricula and teaching in similar ways have often been met with hesitation.
  • How do we incorporate the critical evaluation of AI output into our courses so that students can robustly check these results?
  • Should we be incorporating formalization techniques such as Lean into our upper-level and proof-based courses?
  • Can we reduce the number of topics within each course to create space to focus on reading and interpreting AI output and comparing the answers it gives to the theory students understand to be true?
  • Can we reduce the focus on arduous computations while continuing to emphasize the procedural fluency necessary to critically analyze mathematical arguments?
  • How do engineering, science, social science, business, and health science disciplines see their mathematics, statistics, and data science educational needs changing in the coming years? We certainly must collaborate with related disciplines to thoughtfully consider how moving away from computation to concept and interpretation impacts the training of their students.
  • How do we create courses that emphasize humanized mathematical and statistical communication?

This list is in no way exhaustive, but we do hope it can jumpstart the conversation.

Faculty in all departments need to be thinking hard about how our curriculum should change, before external players force change upon us. Continued leadership from mathematical organizations, including the AMS and MAA, as well as private organizations, is needed. The federal government would also be well-served by offering grants to support the development of innovative mathematics curricula for the AI era. After all, AI technology does not exist without the work of mathematicians. Together, we can work to give our students what they are owed: an education that prepares them to enter a world where they can effectively use AI as a tool, but not as a crutch.

item.title: Futures of Maths Launch
item.dc:creator: Terence Tao
item.description: [This is a guest post by Francesco Fournier-Facio, Yara Kyrychenko, Jon Roozenbeek, and Julian Wykowski, cross-posted from the Proofs and Prompts blog. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] Today we launch Futures of Maths, a new, living platform that asks active research mathematicians about […]
item.content:encoded:
[This is a guest post by Francesco Fournier-Facio, Yara Kyrychenko, Jon Roozenbeek, and Julian Wykowski, cross-posted from the Proofs and Prompts blog. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

Today we launch Futures of Maths, a new, living platform that asks active research mathematicians about the most pressing questions around maths and AI. A string of solutions to famous maths problems, found with the help of AI, has provoked a great deal of discussion among research mathematicians. We built Futures of Maths to understand how mathematicians are dealing with this change in their research and teaching, and where they see the field heading.

How it works. The platform shows you short statements about maths and AI. You rate each one from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree”, or skip it, and you can mark the ones you find exceptionally important. Once you have answered, you see how everyone has rated the statement so far. You don’t have to finish in one go: you can leave and come back at any time. Most importantly, you can post your own statements. A moderator checks each one, and then everyone else can rate it, so the set of statements keeps evolving with the community’s input.

Results. Once we have collected enough responses, we will publish the results and make them available to the community. We will post again on Proofs and Prompts when this happens.

Who can participate. You can take part if you are 18 or older and have at least one article published in the last 5 years in a mathematics journal, meaning one indexed by zbMATH Open (recently accepted articles also count). The quickest way in is to sign in with ORCID. The article must be on your public ORCID record, added by Crossref. Articles you enter yourself don’t count. If it isn’t there, accept Crossref’s permission request in your ORCID inbox and make the work public. If that doesn’t work, for example because your article is accepted but not yet published, you can request a manual review from your institutional email address. We review these case by case.
We appreciate that this is only an approximation of what an active research mathematician is, but we chose it for its simplicity, objectivity and efficient verifiability. We welcome proposals of alternative criteria that cover a more representative sample, and have these same three qualities, they could be implemented in future iterations.

Privacy. The survey is anonymous. Verification happens on a separate website, and the survey itself never learns your name, email address or ORCID iD. When you first register, you receive a personal link that lets you return as often as you like as the consultation evolves. Please save this link. We can’t look it up or resend it, because that is what keeps you anonymous. Questions about yourself are optional, under “My session”, and you can withdraw your answers at any time.

Inviting wide participation. The results will only be meaningful if a large and diverse group of people takes part, both proposing statements and rating them. Please share this widely, and especially with people whose point of view you feel is underrepresented in the discussion on maths and AI.

If you have any suggestions or feature requests, please leave them in the comments!

My own views on these topics (which often overlap with, but are not identical to, those of the guest authors) are summarized on this page. item.content:encoded:
[This is a guest post by the AHM communications group. — T.]

We are happy to announce that the Teaching Working Group of the Association for Human Mathematics wrote a set of recommendations on doctoral advising aimed at departments, advisors, and students. The document contains five guidelines centered on prioritizing human-authored writing, avoiding overreliance on AI, confronting the ethical concerns of AI use, and improving the wellbeing of students, as well as concrete proposals on how to implement them. We encourage everyone to read and share the document, and we especially look forward to feedback and suggestions.
